claim: Airborne viruses such as SARS-CoV-2 with the ability to rapidly mutate combined with high rates of transmission and fatality can cause a deadly worldwide pandemic in a matter of weeks.
source: COVID19 has aptly revealed that airborne viruses such as SARS-CoV-2 with the ability to rapidly mutate combined with high rates of transmission and fatality can cause a deadly worldwide pandemic in a matter of weeks (Plato et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Plato et al., 2021, which provides scholarly support for this assertion about SARS-CoV-2's pandemic potential.

claim: Real-time genomic surveillance based on mutation analysis of viral proteins can be used for a priori determination of surge in number of infection cases.
source: We describe here real-time genomic surveillance particularly based on mutation analysis, of viral proteins as a methodology for a priori determination of surge in number of infection cases.
evidence: This is a primary claim of the manuscript describing their methodological approach. The claim is supported by data presented in the figures showing correlations between mutations and surges.

claim: The full results for SARS-CoV-2 are available at http://pandemics.okstate.edu/covid19/ and are updated daily as new virus sequences become available.
source: The full results are available for SARS-CoV-2 at http://pandemics.okstate.edu/covid19/, and are updated daily as new virus sequences become available.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the availability and update frequency of their results on a specific website.

claim: The genomic surveillance approach is generic and will be applicable to other pathogens.
source: This approach is generic and will also be applicable to other pathogens.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the generalizability of their approach to other pathogens beyond SARS-CoV-2.

claim: Protein and genome sequence analyses identify molecular level changes that enable viral adaptations for increased spread through the host population.
source: Protein and genome sequence analyses identify molecular level changes that enable viral adaptations for increased spread through the host population.
evidence: This claim draws on established scientific knowledge about how sequence analysis can reveal viral adaptations.

claim: Concrete evidence for a direct relationship between specific mutations and increase in rates of infection (and fatality) requires extensive laboratory studies that need significant time.
source: Concrete evidence for a direct relationship between specific mutations and increase in rates of infection (and fatality) requires extensive laboratory studies that need significant time.
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge about the requirements for establishing causal relationships in virology.

claim: The availability of unprecedented number of SARS-CoV-2 genome sequences is making possible identification of number and types of mutations.
source: The availability of unprecedented number of SARS-CoV-2 genome sequences is making possible identification of number and types of mutations, which in turn can provide vital knowledge in real time, crucial for decision making by health professionals for medical interventions.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data described in the manuscript showing analysis of over 6.4 million sequences.

claim: The authors are investigating several different approaches (synonymous, non-synonymous, and non-synonymous/synonymous ratio for the nucleotide sequences and conservative or radical substitutions for the amino acid sequences) for using number and types of mutations as a means to predict surge in infections.
source: We are investigating several different approaches (synonymous, non-synonymous, and non-synonymous/synonymous ratio for the nucleotide sequences [Zhang et al., 2006] and conservative or radical substitutions for the amino acid sequences) for using number and types of mutations as a means to predict surge in infections as well as to monitor the changes in critical viral proteins.
evidence: This describes the methodological approaches being investigated, with citation support for the Ka/Ks ratio approach.

claim: Recently, mutation analysis has been reported for single SARS-CoV-2 proteins.
source: Recently, such analysis has been reported for single SARS-CoV-2 proteins (Kistler et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kistler et al., 2022.

claim: The authors' approach is based on the whole viral genome analysis and is performed continually in real time.
source: Our approach, however, is based on the whole viral genome analysis and moreover it is performed continually in real time.
evidence: This describes a key distinguishing feature of their approach compared to prior work, supported by their data collection and analysis methods.

claim: Data for the number of reported COVID19 cases was accessed from Johns Hopkins University's Our World In Data project.
source: Data for the number of reported COVID19 cases was accessed from Johns Hopkins University's Our World In Data project (https://ourworldindata.org/coronavirus-source-data) (Dong et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a factual statement about their data source, supported by citation.

claim: An in-house pipeline of scripts was designed around the eUtils tools from NCBI to download and process SARS-CoV-2 records from NCBI's GenBank.
source: An in-house pipeline of scripts (using Linux commands) was designed around the eUtils tools (Nadkarni and Parikh, 2012) from NCBI in order to download and process the SARS-CoV-2 records from NCBI's GenBank (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/genbank/).
evidence: This describes their computational methodology with citation support for the eUtils tools.

claim: As of November 21, 2022, a total of 6,468,196 records were searched and a total of 3,126,129 sequences matching the search criterion and passing the quality control steps were used for the results.
source: Collectively as of November 21, 2022, a total of 6,468,196 records were searched and a total of 3,126,129 sequences matching the search criterion and passing the quality control steps were used for the results presented here .
evidence: This is a factual statement about the data analyzed in the study.

claim: Incomplete and ambiguous SARS-CoV-2 genomic sequences and records containing incomplete collection dates were filtered out using the designed pipeline.
source: Incomplete and ambiguous SARS-CoV-2 genomic sequences and records containing incomplete collection dates were filtered out using the designed pipeline.
evidence: This describes their quality control methodology.

claim: As of July 2022, the described sources are monitored daily for updates.
source: As of July 2022, the described sources are monitored daily for updates.
evidence: This is a factual statement about their data monitoring frequency.

claim: The translated proteins and nucleotides sequences were aligned using clustal-omega and Pal2Nal programs.
source: The translated proteins and nucleotides sequences were aligned using clustal-omega (Sievers and Higgins, 2014) and Pal2Nal (Suyama et al., 2006) programs to align the codons with their associated amino acids.
evidence: This describes their alignment methodology with citations to the software tools used.

claim: The resulting alignments were processed through the program kaks_calculator to calculate non-synonymous (Ka) and synonymous (Ks) values, and their ratio (Ka/Ks).
source: The resulting alignments were then processed through the program kaks_calculator (Zhang, 2022) to calculate non-synonymous (Ka) and synonymous (Ks) values, and their ratio (Ka/Ks) which were used to assess the mutational adaptation for each protein.
evidence: This describes their computational analysis method with citation support.

claim: The parameters required for the kaks_calculator were based on the maximum-likelihood method derived from the work of Goldman and Yang, 1994.
source: The parameters required for the kaks_calculator were based on the maximum-likelihood method derived from the work of Goldman and Yang, 1994.
evidence: This describes the specific parameters used in their analysis, supported by citation.

claim: The first reported SARS-CoV-2 genomic sequence ('the Wuhan sequence') was used as a reference for all the Ka, Ks, and Ka/Ks calculations.
source: The first reported SARS-CoV-2 genomic sequence ('the Wuhan sequence') (Wu et al., 2020) was used as a reference for all the Ka, Ks, and Ka/Ks calculations.
evidence: This describes their choice of reference sequence with citation support.

claim: Using the Wuhan sequence as a reference provided the most intuitive and interpretable results.
source: It was also found that using the Wuhan sequence as a reference provided the most intuitive and interpretable results.
evidence: This is an inference based on their exploration of different reference sequence options.

claim: Collective non-synonymous mutations in key proteins of SARS-CoV-2 showed significant increase 10–14 days before the rapid rise in COVID19 cases, particularly related to the surges that occurred after the emergence of Gamma, Delta, Omicron, and BA.5 variants.
source: It was found that collective non-synonymous mutations in key proteins of SARS-CoV-2 showed significant increase 10–14 days before the rapid rise in COVID19 cases, particularly related to the surges that occurred after the emergence of Gamma, Delta, Omicron, and BA.5 variants (Figure 1 and the related Figure 1—figure supplement 1 with the unnormalized results).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by data shown in Figure 1 and its supplement.

claim: Over 6.4 million SARS-CoV-2 genome sequences collected all over the world are available from GenBank.
source: At present, over 6.4 million SARS-CoV-2 genome sequences collected all over the world are available from GenBank (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/sars-cov-2/), which were used for analysis of 26 SARS-CoV-2 proteins, including the structural (spike, envelope, membrane, nucleocapsid) proteins, non-structural proteins (NSPs), and ORFs.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the data available and analyzed.

claim: The analysis was performed with the first reported ('Wuhan') SARS-CoV-2 sequence as a reference.
source: Note, our analysis was performed with the first reported ('Wuhan') SARS-CoV-2 sequence as a reference (Wu et al., 2020).
evidence: This describes their analytical approach with citation support.

claim: The computed mutations are calculated in comparison to the Wuhan reference sequence.
source: In other words, the computed mutations are calculated in comparison to this reference sequence.
evidence: This clarifies their computational approach.

claim: The reason for an increase in mutations ahead of a surge is the search for adaptation against the acquired immunity (or gain in function) in either a single protein or a combination of proteins.
source: The reason for an increase in mutations ahead of a surge is the search for adaptation against the acquired immunity (or gain in function) in either a single protein or a combination of proteins.
evidence: This is an inference about the biological mechanism underlying the observed pattern, based on established knowledge of viral evolution.

claim: The case of the Omicron variant indicates the development of the most drastic changes in several different proteins, which coincided with the largest increase in rate of infections.
source: The case of the Omicron variant indicates the development of the most drastic changes in several different proteins, which coincided with the largest increase in rate of infections (Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Non-synonymous mutations (Ka) in several proteins show significant increase before the increase in rate of infections (or surges), therefore, allowing a means for surge prediction.
source: Non-synonymous mutations (Ka) in several proteins show significant increase before the increase in rate of infections (or surges), therefore, allowing a means for surge prediction.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study, supported by the data presented in the figures.

claim: The mutation values have been normalized using average of all mutations in the year 2020 (the first full year of the pandemic) as 1.
source: The mutation values have been normalized using average of all mutations in the year 2020 (the first full year of the pandemic) as 1 (marked by dashed lines).
evidence: This describes the normalization method used in Figure 1.

claim: Values of 0 indicate same sequence as the Wuhan sequence, while larger values indicate more mutations.
source: Values of 0 indicate same sequence as the Wuhan sequence, while larger values indicate more mutations.
evidence: This explains the interpretation of the mutation values in their analysis.

claim: Each gray dot corresponds to a unique sequence, and there can be multiple records showing the same mutation.
source: Note that each gray dot corresponds to a unique sequence, and there can be multiple records showing the same mutation.
evidence: This clarifies the representation of data in Figure 1.

claim: The weighted mean for the day is calculated by using all sequences reported for the day.
source: The weighted mean for the day is calculated by using all sequences reported for the day.
evidence: This describes the calculation method for the black lines in Figure 1.

claim: Alpha/Beta, Omicron, and Omicron BA.2, BA.5 were the prevalent variants at the time of labeled peaks.
source: Alpha/Beta, Omicron, and Omicron BA.2, BA.5 were the prevalent variants at the time of labeled peaks.
evidence: This is a factual statement about which variants were prevalent during specific peaks shown in Figure 1.

claim: For the two peaks in 2021 the case was less clear, with Gamma and Delta variants being observed at different times in different parts of the world.
source: For the two peaks in 2021 the case was less clear, with Gamma and Delta variants being observed at different times in different parts of the world.
evidence: This acknowledges uncertainty in variant attribution for specific peaks.

claim: Ka/Ks did not provide a reliable signal for surge prediction.
source: In particular, the commonly used non-synonymous to synonymous mutations ratio, Ka/Ks (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), and the rate of mutations (derivative of observed number of mutations with respect to time) (Figure 1—figure supplement 3) were also investigated in detail for suitability as a signal for surge prediction. As seen in Figure 1—figure supplement 2, Ka/Ks did not provide a reliable surge prediction signal.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The ratio for only the membrane protein shows increase before the surges associated with some variants.
source: The ratio for only the membrane protein shows increase before the surges associated with some variants.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: For the case of Omicron surge, the proteins did show increased rate of mutations, however, for all other cases a clear signal was absent.
source: Figure 1—figure supplement 3 shows rate of mutations (calculated as a numerical derivative). For the case of Omicron surge, the proteins did show increased rate of mutations, however, for all other cases a clear signal was absent.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: The nature of incoming genomic data is generally noisy (due to smaller number of samples and weighting of different mutations shows large variations) and changes quickly.
source: Second, the nature of incoming genomic data is generally noisy (due to smaller number of samples and weighting of different mutations shows large variations) and changes quickly, therefore, the ongoing most recent rate of mutations is very noisy as well.
evidence: This is an observation about the characteristics of the data being analyzed.

claim: At this stage, rate (derivative) of mutations is not a reliable signal for surge prediction.
source: It was concluded that at this stage, rate (derivative) of mutations is not a reliable signal for surge prediction.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on their analysis of the rate of mutations approach.

claim: Collective non-synonymous mutations (Ka) provides the most reliable signal for surge prediction.
source: Overall, it appears that collective non-synonymous mutations (Ka) provides the most reliable signal for surge prediction.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion based on comparison of different metrics.

claim: Spike protein interacts with the angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 receptor and plays a vital role in infecting the human cells.
source: Spike protein interacts with the angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 receptor and plays a vital role in infecting the human cells (Xia, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to established knowledge about spike protein function.

claim: Spike protein has been the target of mRNA-based vaccines.
source: Spike protein has been the target of mRNA-based vaccines.
evidence: This is established knowledge about COVID-19 vaccine design.

claim: Viral sequences show significant changes in synonymous and non-synonymous mutations in the spike protein (188,166 unique sequences observed so far).
source: Viral sequences show significant changes in synonymous and non-synonymous mutations in the spike protein (188,166 unique sequences observed so far), with large increases ahead of the surge in reported human infections, most noticeably with the surges associated with the Gamma/Delta and the Omicron variants (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1A and the number of unique sequences analyzed.

claim: The mutations show increase 10–14 days before the increase in human infections.
source: It is important to note that the mutations show increase 10–14 days before the increase in human infections.
evidence: This is a key finding supported by the temporal patterns shown in Figure 1.

claim: The synonymous mutations show decrease post surges.
source: It is also interesting to note that the synonymous mutations (data available on the website) show decrease post surges.
evidence: This observation is based on data available on their website.

claim: The decrease in mutations prior to the Omicron BA.2 surge corresponds to reversal mutations (returning to reference sequence).
source: The decrease in mutations prior to the Omicron BA.2 surge corresponds to reversal mutations (returning to reference sequence).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed decrease in mutations.

claim: At present the non-synonymous and synonymous mutations post the Omicron variant remain elevated, more so than any period during the COVID19 outbreak.
source: However, at present the non-synonymous and synonymous mutations post the Omicron variant remain elevated, more so than any period during the COVID19 outbreak.
evidence: This is an observation based on the data shown in Figure 1.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 membrane protein has shown significant mutations, starting just before the Omicron variant (November 2021 onward).
source: In addition to the spike protein, SARS-CoV-2 membrane (Lu et al., 2021; Figure 1B, 11,338 unique sequences observed so far) and envelope (Zheng et al., 2021; Figure 1C, 1314 unique sequences observed so far) proteins have also shown significant mutations, starting just before the Omicron variant (November 2021 onward).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1B and citations.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 envelope protein has shown significant mutations, starting just before the Omicron variant (November 2021 onward).
source: In addition to the spike protein, SARS-CoV-2 membrane (Lu et al., 2021; Figure 1B, 11,338 unique sequences observed so far) and envelope (Zheng et al., 2021; Figure 1C, 1314 unique sequences observed so far) proteins have also shown significant mutations, starting just before the Omicron variant (November 2021 onward).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1C and citations.

claim: For the case of membrane protein, there was a significant increase that started in the Gamma/Delta variants (June 2021 onward) and further increased just before the BA.5 surge.
source: For the case of membrane protein, there was a significant increase that started in the Gamma/Delta variants (June 2021 onward) and further increased just before the BA.5 surge.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The spike, membrane, and envelope proteins are all located on the surface of SARS-CoV-2 and potentially interact with the components of the immune system.
source: The spike, membrane, and envelope proteins are all located on the surface of SARS-CoV-2 and potentially interact with the components of the immune system.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of SARS-CoV-2 structure and function.

claim: The large increase in mutations in all these external proteins assumes importance in post-vaccination period.
source: The large increase in mutations in all these external proteins assumes importance in post-vaccination period (discussed further below).
evidence: This is an inference about the significance of the observed mutations in the context of vaccination.

claim: RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RDRP) has been targeted for development of antiviral drug therapies.
source: For comparison, Figure 1D shows mutations from RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RDRP, 60,575 unique sequences observed so far), which has been targeted for development of antiviral drug therapies.
evidence: This is established knowledge about RDRP as a drug target.

claim: Till present, RDRP has shown comparatively lower magnitude of non-synonymous mutations.
source: Till present, RDRP has shown comparatively lower magnitude of non-synonymous mutations.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Significant increases in mutations are also observed in NSPs 1, 4, 6, 13, 15, ORFs 6, 7a, and 7b.
source: Significant increases in mutations are also observed in NSPs 1, 4, 6, 13, 15, ORFs 6, 7a, and 7b (data available on the project website).
evidence: This claim is based on data available on their website.

claim: Widespread vaccination against SARS-CoV-2 (December 2020 onward) coincides with significant increase in mutation rates of several SARS-CoV-2 proteins.
source: Widespread vaccination against SARS-CoV-2 (December 2020 onward) coincides with significant increase in mutation rates of several SARS-CoV-2 proteins.
evidence: This is an observation of temporal correlation between vaccination rollout and mutation rates.

claim: Spike, membrane, and envelope proteins have shown rapid mutations especially in the Omicron variant.
source: Spike, membrane, and envelope proteins have shown rapid mutations especially in the Omicron variant (gray dots in Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The rapid mutations in spike, membrane, and envelope proteins are possibly due to viral adaptations under the selective pressure exerted by the vaccine.
source: This is possibly due to viral adaptations under the selective pressure exerted by the vaccine, as a significant number of mutations were observed in 2021, especially for the spike protein (gray dots in Figure 1A indicate spike protein has mutated much more than any other protein).
evidence: This is a speculative inference about the mechanism driving the observed mutations, based on evolutionary principles.

claim: The long-term effectiveness of mRNA-based SARS-CoV-2 vaccines remains unknown.
source: The long-term effectiveness of mRNA-based SARS-CoV-2 vaccines remains unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge regarding vaccine effectiveness.

claim: After the initial regimen of two doses, the administration of additional booster (third and fourth) doses has decreased due to improvement in COVID19 fatality rates as well as political reasons.
source: After the initial regimen of two doses, the administration of additional booster (third and fourth) doses has decreased due to improvement in COVID19 fatality rates as well as political reasons (Sabahelzain et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation and reflects observed trends in vaccination practices.

claim: Post vaccination the significant mutations observed in the spike, envelope, and membrane protein related to the Omicron variant remain at extremely elevated levels.
source: Other proteins have shown reversal mutations (higher similarity with the reference sequence) after periods of significant increase in mutations, however, post vaccination the significant mutations observed in the spike, envelope, and membrane protein related to the Omicron variant remain at extremely elevated levels.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Omicron, BA.2, BA.5, and subsequent variants are showing increased rates of transmission.
source: As Omicron, BA.2, BA.5, and subsequent variants are showing increased rates of transmission, gain or improvement of function in other proteins could lead to emergence of newer variants of concern.
evidence: This is based on observed epidemiological data about variant transmission.

claim: Gain or improvement of function in other proteins could lead to emergence of newer variants of concern.
source: As Omicron, BA.2, BA.5, and subsequent variants are showing increased rates of transmission, gain or improvement of function in other proteins could lead to emergence of newer variants of concern.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about future variant emergence based on evolutionary principles.

claim: Over long term this needs to be addressed by vaccines with longer periods of effectiveness and post-infection treatment options including antiviral drugs.
source: Over long term this needs to be addressed by vaccines with longer periods of effectiveness and post-infection treatment options including antiviral drugs.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the implications of their findings.

claim: To date, spike protein has shown the most direct correlation in the rate of non-synonymous mutations and the rates of human infection.
source: To date, spike protein has shown the most direct correlation in the rate of non-synonymous mutations and the rates of human infection.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on their analysis of multiple proteins.

claim: In the case of Omicron variant and also the Gamma variant, spike protein showed rapid increase in mutations about 10–14 days ahead of time.
source: In particular, in the case of Omicron variant and also the Gamma variant, spike protein showed rapid increase in mutations about 10–14 days ahead of time.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Membrane protein showed rapid mutations before surge related to BA.5.
source: Furthermore, membrane protein showed rapid mutations before surge related to BA.5.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The authors issued a surge watch on the website on June 29, 2022, which was converted to a warning on July 14.
source: For example, we issued a surge watch on the website on June 29, 2022, which was converted to a warning on July 14.
evidence: This is a factual statement about actions taken by the authors.

claim: The surge watch issued on June 29, 2022 was confirmed by increase in infection cases worldwide throughout July.
source: This was confirmed by increase in infection cases worldwide throughout July (see Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: The authors issued an additional warning on September 7, 2022, which was confirmed by surge in several European countries, including France, United Kingdom, Germany, and Italy.
source: Further, we issued an additional warning on September 7, 2022, which was confirmed by surge in several European countries, including France, United Kingdom, Germany, and Italy (see Figure 1—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 6.

claim: The role of different (or dominant) SARS-CoV-2 variants in major surges is unclear at this time and needs further research.
source: The role of different (or dominant) SARS-CoV-2 variants in major surges is unclear at this time and needs further research.
evidence: This acknowledges a limitation in current understanding.

claim: Different variants have been prevalent in different geographic regions at different times over the course of COVID19 outbreak.
source: Different variants have been prevalent in different geographic regions at different times over the course of COVID19 outbreak, therefore, it is difficult to assign the surges to individual variants.
evidence: This is based on epidemiological knowledge about variant distribution.

claim: At present the authors' analysis is able to make predictions about collective surges before they occur, as illustrated by the case of BA.5.
source: However, at present our analysis is able to make predictions about collective surges before they occur, as illustrated by the case of BA.5.
evidence: This claim is supported by their successful prediction of the BA.5 surge.

claim: As the pandemic situation has improved in the second half of 2022, the number of tests being performed and the sequences being deposited into public repositories have decreased.
source: In particular, as the pandemic situation has improved in the second half of 2022, the number of tests being performed and the sequences being deposited into public repositories have decreased.
evidence: This is an observation about trends in data availability.

claim: The population is showing increased immunity against the virus due to vaccination and naturally acquired immunity.
source: Furthermore, it is widely being discussed that the population is showing increased immunity against the virus due to vaccination and naturally acquired immunity.
evidence: This reflects current scientific discourse about population immunity.

claim: The presented approach is dependent on availability of sequences.
source: The presented approach is dependent on availability of sequences, therefore, we hope that scientific community will continue to urge the medical community and public health agencies to commit resources to sequencing the samples from COVID19 positive patients on a regular basis.
evidence: This is a statement about a limitation of their approach.

claim: Even with availability of smaller number of sequences, the approach is weighted by mutations and percentage of sequences showing non-synonymous mutations.
source: Nonetheless, even with availability of smaller number of sequences, our approach is weighted by mutations and percentage of sequences showing non-synonymous mutations.
evidence: This describes a feature of their methodology that provides some robustness.

claim: Whenever new mutations show up in large percentages, the approach will still be able to work.
source: Therefore, whenever new mutations show up in large percentages, our approach will still be able to work.
evidence: This is an inference about the robustness of their approach under different data availability scenarios.

claim: Viruses continue to evolve.
source: On the other hand, viruses continue to evolve and if the population acquires large-scale immunity leading to drastic reduction in number of infections, our surveillance approach would still allow preparation in cases of significant viral genome changes (such as going from SARS-CoV to SARS-CoV-2) whenever they occur and lead to the possibility of another major outbreak.
evidence: This is established knowledge about viral evolution.

claim: The surveillance approach would still allow preparation in cases of significant viral genome changes whenever they occur and lead to the possibility of another major outbreak.
source: On the other hand, viruses continue to evolve and if the population acquires large-scale immunity leading to drastic reduction in number of infections, our surveillance approach would still allow preparation in cases of significant viral genome changes (such as going from SARS-CoV to SARS-CoV-2) whenever they occur and lead to the possibility of another major outbreak.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the future utility of their approach.

claim: The methodology and the website provide real-time mutational changes of 26 SARS-CoV-2 proteins and ORFs.
source: The methodology and the website described here provide real-time mutational changes of 26 SARS-CoV-2 proteins and ORFs.
evidence: This is a factual statement about what their system provides.

claim: The changes in non-synonymous mutations correlate with the increase in reported cases of infections.
source: The changes in non-synonymous mutations correlate with the increase in reported cases of infections.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by data in Figure 1.

claim: The website is intended to keep the medical community informed about potential upcoming surges.
source: Apart from identifying mutations of concern for in-depth scientific studies, the website is intended to keep the medical community informed about potential upcoming surges.
evidence: This describes the intended purpose of their website.

claim: Warnings of increase in mutations and expected surges are displayed on the website (and also available through email alerts).
source: Warnings of increase in mutations and expected surges are displayed on the website (and also available through email alerts).
evidence: This is a factual statement about features of their website.

claim: This real-time analysis is dependent on the various health labs and medical facilities for swiftly depositing the viral genome sequences into the public databases such as the GenBank.
source: It should be noted that this real-time analysis is dependent on the various health labs and medical facilities for swiftly depositing the viral genome sequences into the public databases such as the GenBank.
evidence: This describes a dependency of their approach on external data sources.

claim: The shorter the lag time in depositing the sequences by the wider community, more accurate and effective the prediction capabilities of the approach and the website will be.
source: The shorter the lag time in depositing the sequences by the wider community, more accurate and effective the prediction capabilities of our approach and the website will be.
evidence: This is an inference about how data timeliness affects prediction accuracy.

claim: The number of infection cases showed a sustained increase after the issue of the watch on June 29.
source: The number of infection cases showed a sustained increase after the issue of our watch on June 29.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: The watch was elevated to a warning on July 14 (note, warning is considered more severe than a watch) and the number of cases showed a further increase.
source: This watch was elevated to a warning on July 14 (note, warning is considered more severe than a watch) and the number of cases showed a further increase.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: The warning was removed on August 30, 2022.
source: The warning was removed on August 30, 2022.
evidence: This is a factual statement about actions taken, shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: The number of cases peaked roughly a month after the watch was issued.
source: The number of cases peaked roughly a month after our watch was issued.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: The number of infection cases showed a sustained increase in Europe and several individual countries, after the watch was issued.
source: The number of infection cases showed a sustained increase in Europe and several individual countries, after we issued our watch.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 6.

claim: The watch issued on September 7, 2022 was eventually removed on November 14, 2022.
source: The data did not warrant a further elevation and this watch was eventually removed on November 14, 2022.
evidence: This is a factual statement about actions taken, shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 6.
